passages.happening:
“To everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven” (verse 1).

Then come fourteen pairs. ‘A time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to uproot’ (verse 2). A time to kill and a time to heal, to break down and to build (verse 3). ‘A time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to mourn and a time to dance’ (verse 4). A time to throw away stones and to gather them, to embrace and to hold back (verse 5). A time to search and to count as lost, to keep and to throw away (verse 6). ‘A time to tear and a time to mend, a time to be silent and a time to speak’ (verse 7). ‘A time to love and a time to hate, a time for war and a time for peace’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
After the royal experiment of chapter 2, the Teacher widens his view. He is no longer asking what a king can achieve but how anyone can live within the rhythms God has set. Chapter 1 described an endless cycle that gets nowhere. Chapter 3 describes a world of seasons, each fitting in its time.

The poem sets opposites side by side, fourteen pairs, twenty-eight times in all. Fourteen is twice seven, the number of completeness, which may suggest that the poem covers the whole range of human life.

Some lines reflect old customs. A time to throw away stones and to gather them may mean clearing a field before planting, or scattering stones on an enemy's field to ruin it, and later Jewish interpreters also read it as a polite way of speaking about married love. The meaning is uncertain. A time to tear and to mend may reflect the custom of tearing clothes in grief and mending them after mourning.

Ancient people lived close to birth and death, planting and harvest, war and peace. The poem describes the seasons of a life as they come. It does not make killing or hating a duty.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: The psalm knows the same turning of seasons: ‘Weeping may stay the night, but joy comes in the morning’ (Psalm 30:5). And Paul asks for the same fitting response to each: ‘Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep’ (Romans 12:15).
passages.asks: There is a time for everything. Ask which season you are in now, weeping or laughing, tearing or mending, silence or speech. And ask whether you are trying to live in a season that is not yours yet, or one that has already passed.

passages.t: Beautiful in its time, and eternity in the heart
passages.happening:
‘What does the worker gain from his toil?’ (verse 9). The Teacher has seen the burden God has given people to keep them busy (verse 10).

“He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in the hearts of men, yet they cannot fathom the work that God has done from beginning to end” (verse 11).

So there is nothing better than to rejoice and do good while they live, ‘and also that every man should eat and drink and find satisfaction in all his labor’ (verse 13), which is God's gift. ‘I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
These verses reflect on the poem. The times belong to God, who has made everything beautiful, or fitting, yapheh, in its time.

Eternity is olam, a long stretch of time, forever. God has put in human hearts a sense of the whole, a longing for what lasts, and yet people cannot see the whole of what God is doing from beginning to end. That is the ache the book keeps naming: made for eternity, living in a moment.

Ideas about a right time for every action were common in ancient wisdom. What is distinctive here is that the times belong to God.

Verse 14 gives a reason for God's ways: that people should fear him. The fear of God, which the book ends with, is already here.
passages.later: Paul says what verse 11 sees: ‘For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen’ (Romans 1:20). And Job's friend confesses the limit: ‘Can you fathom the deep things of God or discover the limits of the Almighty?’ (Job 11:7).
passages.asks: God has set eternity in human hearts. Ask what longing in you nothing under the sun has satisfied. And ask where you can trust that God is making things beautiful in their time, even when you cannot see the whole.

passages.happening:
‘Furthermore, I saw under the sun that in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness’ (verse 16). The Teacher says to himself that God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, since there is a time for every deed (verse 17).

Then he faces death. People and animals share one fate: as one dies, so does the other, and they all have the same breath (verse 19). ‘All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust’ (verse 20). ‘Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?’ (verse 21).

And he ends where chapter 2 ended: ‘I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot’ (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Verse 16 could fit any period of Israel's history. The prophets condemned corrupt courts in both kingdoms, and the later centuries had their share of distant and corrupt officials. Human justice fails, and it fails even where it should be strongest. Verse 17 holds on to the one hope left: God will judge.

The question ‘Who knows’ in verse 21 is typical of the Teacher's honesty about the limits of what he can see.
passages.later: Behind verse 20 stands Genesis: ‘For dust you are, and to dust you shall return’ (Genesis 3:19). And the book later answers the Teacher's question in part: ‘the spirit returns to God who gave it’ (Ecclesiastes 12:7).
passages.hard:
Does verse 19 teach that humans are no different from animals and that there is no life after death?

Verses 18 to 21 say that humans and animals share one fate and one breath and return to the same dust, and they ask who knows whether the human spirit goes upward. Some readers take this as the Teacher's denial of any afterlife, or at least his doubt about it.

Notice what he says and what he does not say. He speaks of what can be seen under the sun: all living things die and decay. He asks who knows, admitting ignorance, not asserting a denial. The Old Testament's light on life after death is limited at first, with clearer hope coming in later texts such as Daniel 12.

The book itself later says that the spirit returns to God who gave it (12:7). Many interpreters read chapter 3 as the Teacher's honest view of death from a human standpoint, which the rest of Scripture answers. Others read it as a deliberate humbling of human pride: people are creatures of dust, depending on God for any hope beyond the grave.
passages.asks: The Teacher asks who knows what lies beyond death. Ask where you have been honest with God about what you do not know. And ask what it would mean to enjoy your work today as your lot from him, since no one can see what comes after.
